analysis.one_liner: Directs trade negotiators to pressure other wealthy nations to drop their prescription drug price controls.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearing, no vote, and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the U.S. Trade Representative to negotiate with the other G-8 countries to eliminate their government price controls on new prescription drugs, on the theory that Americans overpay because those countries only pay the marginal cost of production and leave the U.S. to cover research and development costs. If negotiations failed within 12 months, the Trade Representative would have to recommend measures to Congress, including possible trade retaliation under the Trade Act of 1974, aimed at closing the gap between US and foreign drug prices. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose global pricing power would be protected if other wealthy nations dropped the price controls that keep drug prices lower there than in the United States. The bill states its goal is lowering US drug prices by making other countries pay a larger share of research and development costs, but the mechanism runs entirely through trade pressure rather than direct price relief for Americans.

how_it_helps.text: Required the U.S. Trade Representative to open negotiations with the other seven G-8 governments to eliminate their price controls on innovative medicines and the 'unfair trade practices' resulting from them

If negotiations had not succeeded within 12 months, the Trade Representative would have had to recommend measures to Congress, including retaliation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, to eliminate the gap between US and foreign drug prices
The bill's stated goal was reducing prescription drug prices for US consumers by forcing other countries to pay a larger share of the research and development costs of new medicines

analysis.who_pays: Foreign governments and their citizens, who would face pressure to abandon price controls and pay higher drug prices; US consumers could also bear costs if trade retaliation raised tariffs or disrupted trade with major partners like Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Italy, and the UK.
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign health systems and US consumers via trade risks

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no direct mechanism to lower drug prices in the United States; its theory is that ending foreign price controls would eventually shift research costs abroad, which is indirect and unproven
The fallback is trade retaliation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 against major allies, which could invite counter-retaliation and raise costs for US exporters and consumers
Pressuring Canada, Japan, and Western Europe to drop their price controls would raise drug prices in those countries without any guaranteed reduction in what Americans pay

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised American consumers cheaper drugs in principle, but its only concrete tools were trade negotiations and the threat of trade retaliation. If the strategy worked as intended, the first effect would be higher drug prices abroad; any reduction for US consumers would depend on drug companies choosing to cut US prices. Meanwhile, retaliation risk would fall on other US industries trading with Canada, Japan, and Europe. The costs were concrete and near-term; the consumer benefit was speculative and distant.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Slade Gorton introduced the bill on April 26, 2000, with introductory remarks but no cosponsors
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign countries' price-control systems and US consumers are unaffected; the main thing avoided was a trade framework that would primarily have protected brand-name drug makers' global pricing power. The sponsor gained nothing beyond a floor statement before leaving office.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign price-control programs and US consumers

for.name: Slade Gorton
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred and no other member signed on, so no partisan pattern can be measured; one Republican senator introduced it and no one else took a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill's main practical effect would be dismantling foreign government price controls, which would let manufacturers charge higher prices in Canada, Europe, and Japan. It contains no mechanism that directly lowers the price Americans pay.

industries.industry: Foreign government drug programs (Canada, Japan, and Western European health systems)
industries.note: These national health systems keep drug prices low by negotiating or setting them. The bill targets their pricing authority as an 'unfair trade practice' and threatens retaliation if they refuse to give it up.

industries.industry: US industries exposed to trade retaliation
industries.note: If negotiations failed, the bill required recommendations for measures under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which can impose tariffs or other trade penalties. Such retaliation could raise costs for US importers and exporters in those markets.
